preamble: Vocalization of the palatal glide [j] to the high front vowel [i], typically when loss of a following vowel leaves the glide in a syllable nucleus or word-final position. In West Germanic, short-stemmed ja-stems such as Proto-Germanic *harjaz "army" lost the ending vowel and the stranded *-j surfaced as *-i (Proto-West Germanic *hari), preserved in Old High German and Old Saxon heri and lowered to -e in Old English here. In Sanskrit the same glide–vowel relationship appears as the samprasāraṇa alternation, in which the ya of roots such as yaj- "sacrifice" is replaced by i in weak forms (iṣṭá). The vowel-to-glide direction (i > j before a vowel) is more frequent.

examples.note: Via Proto-West Germanic *hari: after loss of *-az the final *-j vocalized to -i, later lowered to -e.
Preserves the vocalized -i unlowered; Old Saxon likewise heri. Contrast Gothic harjis, which keeps the glide.
Samprasāraṇa: the ya of the root is replaced by i in weak forms. This is an inherited ablaut alternation rather than a datable sound change.
